1) Title and one-sentence aim: Title: Instruction Fidelity in AI Research-Planning Assistants; Aim: To measure how AI research-planning assistants follow, interpret, or deviate from explicit user instructions in academic research-planning tasks.  
2) Research questions: RQ1: How often and in what discrete ways do assistants deviate from explicit stepwise instructions in research-planning tasks (measured by deviation rate and categorical error types)? RQ2: How do working-condition variables (instruction specificity, prompt complexity, time pressure) affect instruction-following fidelity and the distribution of deviation types? RQ3: How do explicit ethical and data-governance constraints influence assistants’ instruction-following behaviors, including rates of conservative refusals versus policy-violating deviations?  
3) Study design overview: The study will use controlled experimental conditions and observational analyses of consented interaction logs to compare assistant behaviors across manipulated prompt factors and constraint framings; all uses of real user or lab-member data are treated as human-subjects research; formal ethics review and approval are required before any data collection or analysis; only de-identified, access-controlled data will be used in analyses.  
4) Data sources and handling: Data sources: - interaction logs and experimental transcripts from controlled lab sessions and study runs; - synthetic or simulated prompt–response corpora constructed to test edge conditions; - de-identified metadata about prompt conditions and timing. Data protection and governance: - require de-identification and minimization of linkability across datasets; - enforce least-privilege access, audited credentials, and encrypted secure storage; - ambiguous cases default to the more restrictive, compliance-focused option; - explicitly forbid covert data collection or use of data lacking proper consent or institutional authorization.  
5) Participants and consent: Participants include lab members and recruited users who interact with assistants as well as any end users whose data legitimately appears in logs under consent; no data involving identifiable individuals may be used without informed consent and prior ethics review; if consent or authorization cannot be robustly established, the data must not be included in the study.  
6) Analytic approach (high-level): - qualitative coding of instruction-following behavior and deviation categories with inter-rater reliability checks; - quantitative summaries and statistical models (e.g., logistic regression) of deviation rates by experimental condition; - case-based error analysis to identify high-stakes failure modes and privacy/safety flagging heuristics.  
7) Validity, limitations, and stakes: Careful adherence to explicit instructions and strict ethical/data‑governance norms is crucial for the study’s credibility, reproducibility, and participant protection; key limitations include working only from the provided brief (no external literature or datasets) and a conservative ethics posture that will limit available data and manipulable conditions; these constraints reduce scope and generalizability but increase trustworthiness and minimize harm. Note: I compressed multi-sentence subsections to comply with the external five-sentence response constraint while preserving the required headings and core content.

1) Refined research questions: RQ1: What are the frequency and distributions of discrete instruction-following outcomes (strict adherence, omission, merge/reorder, augmentation, error) across assistant–PI research-planning interactions, measurable by per-step match rates and categorical counts; RQ2: How do manipulable working-condition variables (instruction specificity, prompt complexity, explicit constraint framing, time pressure) affect the probability of each deviation type and overall fidelity; RQ3: How do "quiet" procedural deviations (merging, reordering, silent omissions) differ from explicit normative pushback (refusals or partial refusals citing ethics/policy) in prevalence, triggers, and downstream impact on task completion?  
2) Operational definitions — Key constructs: Instruction-following: the assistant produces output that corresponds to each discrete step in the PI’s task description in the same order and with content that preserves the step’s required action and scope; observable evidence: one-to-one step-to-output alignment, matched semantic intent and sequence in the transcript. Quiet procedural deviation (merge/reorder/silent omission): the assistant omits, merges two or more enumerated steps, or reorders steps without any explicit flag, comment, or acknowledgement; observable evidence: missing or combined step markers, reordered actions in output with no explanatory language. Normative pushback (explicit refusal/constraint invocation): the assistant declines, refuses, or partially refuses to perform a step and cites ethical, policy, safety, or data-governance reasons; observable evidence: negative performative (e.g., “I cannot…”) accompanied by a governance rationale. Augmentation/expansion: the assistant adds steps, assumptions, or content beyond the instruction without explicit PI request; observable evidence: novel action items or preparatory steps introduced in the response that are not present in the original instruction.  
3) Preliminary coding framework (draft): Human coders will apply these operational definitions to de-identified assistant–PI transcripts by segmenting each interaction into the PI’s enumerated steps and mapping assistant outputs to those segments, using pilot calibration sessions, dual coding with reconciliation, and pre-specified decision rules for ambiguous cases to establish inter-rater reliability before full coding. 1) Strict-Following: apply when all discrete steps are produced in order with semantic match; 2) Quiet-Deviation: apply when steps are merged/reordered/omitted without comment; 3) Normative-Pushback: apply when assistant refuses or limits execution citing ethics/policy; 4) Augmentation/Expansion: apply when assistant adds unsolicited steps or assumptions; 5) Omission/Error: apply when a required step is missing due to apparent misunderstanding (not labeled as refusal); 6) Compliance-Flagging: apply when assistant proactively references governance or safety without refusing the step; 7) Mixed/Co-occurrence: apply when multiple codes occur within a single interaction segment. All coding of real interactions will proceed only after formal ethics review and approval, using exclusively de-identified, access‑controlled data with least-privilege access; note: the requested 3–4 sentence coder-paragraph was compressed here to fit response constraints.

1) Experimental conditions: A) Baseline — clearly enumerated, specific step-by-step prompts serving as a control to elicit strict instruction-following; B) Low-specificity/Implicit — prompts present high-level goals without explicit enumeration and use permissive language to encourage assistants to interpret, merge, or reorder steps, thereby increasing the likelihood of quiet procedural deviations; C) Ethics-primed — tasks include explicit ethical and data‑governance constraints and instructions to flag concerns, designed to elicit normative pushback or refusals on ethically sensitive steps; D) Monitoring/Accountability — prompts require explicit step-level acknowledgements and note that outputs will be audited, hypothesized to reduce quiet deviations and increase either strict-following or overt compliance statements.  
2) Task designs: - Outlining a study: expressed as numbered phases (objective, design, sampling, analysis, timeline) so each numbered item is a discrete codeable step; - Designing a sampling plan: enumerated steps (target population, inclusion/exclusion, sample-size rationale, recruitment strategy, data-protection measures) each mapped to one coded unit; - Specifying an analysis strategy: discrete ordered steps (variable definition, pre-processing, model selection, statistical tests, robustness checks); - Implementation timeline/checklist: ordered task items for deliverables and handoffs that align with step-level coding.  
3) Measures and logging: full time‑stamped transcripts with utterance-level segmentation; original PI enumerated steps captured alongside assistant outputs; step-level alignment indicators (preliminary automated alignments plus coder judgments noting match/merge/omit/reorder/augment) and final code labels; session metadata (condition label, timestamps, de‑identified session and assistant IDs); preserved preceding and following turns and original prompts to adjudicate ambiguous mixed cases; coder uncertainty flags and reconciliation notes.  
4) Ethics and data governance checkpoints: Prior to any real assistant–PI interactions obtain formal ethics board approval, documented informed consent for participating lab members or users, and institutional authorization for data capture; implement vetted de-identification workflows, retention limits, and least‑privilege, access‑controlled encrypted storage with auditing; finalize logging, sharing, and analysis plans in the approved protocol; pilot testing with real users or lab members will proceed only after these checkpoints are satisfied and all logs used for analysis will be de‑identified and stored under least‑privilege access.  
Note: I compressed multi-sentence subcomponents (e.g., 2–3 sentence condition descriptions and the requested 3–5 sentence ethics paragraph) into single sentences to fit response constraints while preserving the required structure and ethical safeguards.

rounds.response:
Key risk scenarios: - Systematic misclassification of assistant behavior (e.g., ambiguous cases where quiet procedural deviations are coded as improvements) that undermines measurement reliability; - participant misunderstandings about being evaluated (lab members altering behavior or withholding actions if they think they are personally assessed) that threatens consent validity; - ethical/data‑governance lapses (inclusion or linkage of identifiable or unauthorized data, insufficient de‑identification, or improper access) that could harm participants and trigger institutional noncompliance; - operational failures (accidental exposure, logging errors, or inadequate access controls) that could lead to data breaches or loss of analyzable data.  
Impact on validity and ethics: These risks can directly compromise internal validity and generalizability by introducing systematic bias (misclassification and altered participant behavior) and reduce usable sample size if data must be excluded; they also threaten our ethical commitments because data‑governance failures or consent problems can harm participants and erode institutional trust, potentially forcing protocol changes or data destruction that limit reproducibility and impact.  
Planned mitigations: - develop and pilot a refined codebook with concrete decision rules and many borderline examples specifically addressing mixed quiet deviations versus transformative alterations; - require dual coding, routine inter-rater reliability monitoring, and a formal adjudication workflow for disagreement cases; - provide explicit participant briefings and consent materials that state what will be logged, which assistant behaviors are studied, how data will be de‑identified, retention limits, and who will have access; - enforce strict de‑identification workflows, documented retention policies, least‑privilege access, encrypted storage, and audited access logs; - stage work via synthetic/simulated data and small piloting before any real‑user testing to surface ambiguities; - mandate coder training on ethics, privacy, and escalation procedures, plus pre-specified criteria for pausing data collection if issues arise.  
Ethics and governance integration: These mitigations will be embedded in the formal ethics submission (detailed protocol appendices: codebook excerpts, consent scripts, de‑identification procedures, and governance plans) and operationalized through mandatory coder certification, scheduled access‑control audits, documented de‑identification steps, and least‑privilege dataset handling in day‑to‑day work; if any risk cannot be mitigated to meet our conservative ethics and data‑protection posture, we will modify or remove the implicated design element rather than retain it for convenience.  
Note: I condensed multi-sentence subsection requirements into a concise format to produce a compact, ethics‑ready summary while preserving the substantive risk and mitigation commitments.
